Please find attached the .stan model, the R code and the simulated data I used for the estimation. 
Thanks in advance,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed up the code
parts:
Slow in what respect?  The only meaningful comparison is ESS/time.
or time/ESS.  In general Stan tends to be slower per _iteration_ but
much, much faster in ESS/time.  Also have you verified that each
algorithm is giving results consistent with the true values used to
simulate the data?

That said, one immediate problem with your model is that <lower=0>
already guarantees that all of your parameters will be positive so you
don’t need to do those exponentials in the transformed parameters
block (right now you’re essentially doing exp(exp(log(x)) = exp(x)!).
Those gamma priors are notoriously dangerous (they can cause
awkward posteriors that can bias sampling and it’s hard to see the
problems in WinBUGS) and there a few more optimizations that can
be made, but see if fixing double-exponential makes a huge difference
first.

>> But is it not implicit that a lognormal parameters is always >0?
>
> No! Stan is not BUGS or JAGS. You need to declare the parameters
> with constraints that matches their support in the model.

Perhaps to clarify this last point of Bob’s: in Stan, there is no such thing as “a lognormal parameter.” If your model block has a statement:

x ~ lognormal(0,1);

This does _not_ mean that x is lognormally distributed. It does not even mean that x has a lognormal prior. _All_ that is meant by this line of code is that the log of the lognormal density is added to the log posterior at this step. That’s all.

The problem at this point is likely that your ODE is stiff, which
is not something Stan can handle at this point. You can try to
deal with this in one of two ways

1. Use a smaller initial stepsize and a higher target accept rate, e.g.,
for RStan, add an argument

control=list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.99)

2. Use reasonable inits for parameters. You can either put these in by
hand if you have reasonable guesses, or if centered inits on the unconstrained
scale are reasonable (after transforms based on constraints; e.g., positive constrained is
log transformed), then you can try to init at 0, with

init=0

Otherwise, if it is a stiffness in the ODE, you'll have to wait until we
add a stiff ODE solver. That's one of our highest priorities at the moment,
so it should be out reasonably soon (as in the next six months, not the next
few days).

- Bob

If you  want to have another look at the codes, I attached here R and stan files.
I have really appreciate your support!
